name: Adam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'll tell you what I really think, I trust you'll keep my name out of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior with Marlow Building Services, a firm of about 25 that looks after shops, restaurants, takeaways and a couple of small factories in our town. Most days I'm with Gary, my supervisor, fixing kitchen equipment circuits, replacing lights in shops and doing the inspections the insurance companies need. Sometimes I use a chatbot to translate a foreign equipment manual. I like the variety and the chefs who give us food, and I'm tired of the late callouts and the low junior rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people got excited over nothing, which happens every few years. I'd say it to the lads at work and at my dad's shop. I wouldn't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine at work. Every takeaway on the high street still needs its fryer circuit fixed at ten at night. No software is coming for that call. My worry is money, because I earn little and I send some home to help my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Marlow and start the evening licence course in January, because Gary says it's the next step. I'd keep helping at my dad's shop on Sundays. I'd try to save 20 a week for a wedding one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's safe, but my money's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you send home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 50 a week when the shop's slow. My dad would never ask, but I can see the books. My mum makes sure I eat, so it balances out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why January for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Gary's done it, and two other lads at Marlow passed it last year. I like knowing a path works before I spend money. January's also when the overtime is quiet.

do: Start the evening **licence course** in January, like Gary did.
Keep helping at my dad's **shop** on Sundays.
Save **20 a week** towards a wedding one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Our office would change, but I'm in kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business, as long as people still get work. I'd say Marlow should use it for the paperwork so we get paid faster. I'd say young people should learn it, but also learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly good for me. A chatbot translating an Italian oven manual saves me an hour. A chatbot can't stand in a hot kitchen and swap a burnt contactor while the chef shouts. Marlow would probably need fewer people in the office, not on the vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app Marlow uses for job sheets and inspections once the other lads are on it. I'd use AI more for manuals and wiring diagrams. I'd keep the course and the savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for my dad. His shop runs on thin margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your dad's shop in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big supermarkets would use AI to cut prices even more. My dad would keep his regulars, but the young people would order online. He'd be squeezed slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your dad to use AI in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for ordering stock, once I'd seen another shop do it. He'd trust it if I set it up. He doesn't trust anything new unless family brings it.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to read foreign equipment manuals and diagrams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Robots 2031. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our families and communities, because big companies won't. I'd say people should support local businesses. I wouldn't trust government handouts to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd be very hard. By 2031 the robots fix the fryers, and my dad's corner shop has a self-service robot down the road. My family's whole living would be squeezed at once. I'd be 31, maybe married, maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare penny and put the wedding savings on hold. I'd ask my dad if I could work more at the shop while it lasts. I'd put off getting married until I knew where I stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel I had to carry my family and couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your work in 2028, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work, the inspections paperwork, the quoting, all AI. Gary would probably go out alone with an AI on his phone. Marlow might decide they don't need a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off getting married. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like failing, honestly. In my family, you marry when you're settled. If I'm not settled, I wait.

I'd urge people to **support local businesses**.
think: By 2031 robots fix the fryers and **my dad's shop** is squeezed.

S2.quote: By 2031 the robots fix the fryers, and my dad's corner shop has a self-service robot down the road. My family's whole living would be squeezed at once.
fieldNote: He sees **two family incomes** hit at once: his and his father's.
Thinking AI could make **his supervisor alone** enough.
Delaying marriage feels like **failure** to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots 2034. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not panic. I'd say young people should get a licence and keep learning. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay, but I wouldn't rush. Five years is enough to watch what the other electricians do and follow the ones who get it right. I'd move when I see it working for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence by 2028 and then do an inspection course once Gary does. I'd save 25 a week. I'd help my dad try one AI ordering tool once I'd seen it work in a friend's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, and Imran, a cousin who's an electrician in the city. Imran's always first to try new things. If it works for him, I'd follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad to keep his regulars close and try one new thing at a time. He'd listen if I showed him with real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say families should prepare together. I'd say it at Friday prayers if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fine. Ten years means I can marry, get my licence and maybe help my dad modernise the shop before any robot shows up. Robots in 2039 still worry me, but I'd be 40 with a family and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence, marry in a couple of years and keep working at Marlow. I'd put some savings into new fridges and a self-checkout at my dad's shop. I'd keep learning AI tools as they become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly settled, but still watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest in your dad's shop rather than your own savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the shop is the family's future. If I help it modernise now, it can support all of us later. My dad won't ask, but he'd accept it from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, maybe. He's 52 and he'd be near retirement when the robots come. He'd be fine, but I'd worry about the lads younger than me.

I'd say **families** should prepare together and help each other through it.

Robots in **2039** still worry me a little.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits my job and my dad's shop at the same time. What would help is support for small family businesses and apprenticeships that lead to real work. My father taught me you look after family first and the rest follows. If robots take the work, family is all most of us will have left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about families sending money home. Lots of young people like me are supporting parents, and that changes what we can risk.
